# Freshman Congressman Trades Apartment for Office Cot to Save Taxpayer Money

WASHINGTON — When most members of Congress head home after a long day of votes and committee hearings, they retreat to apartments or condos scattered across the nation's capital. But for freshman Rep. Jason Chaffetz (R-Utah), "home" is a folding cot tucked into the corner of his Capitol Hill office.

Since arriving in Washington earlier this year, Chaffetz has forgone renting an apartment altogether, choosing instead to sleep in his own congressional office. It's an arrangement that might seem unusual, even uncomfortable, to outsiders — but for the Utah Republican, it's a simple matter of practicality and principle.

"I didn't come to Washington to live large," Chaffetz has said of the decision. "I came here to do a job, and I don't need a fancy apartment to do it."

The logistics of his living situation are modest by design. Each night, Chaffetz unfolds his cot in his office after the day's business winds down. For his morning routine, he heads to the House gym, which offers showers available to members and staff — a perk that effectively serves as his bathroom. Snacks and light provisions are kept stashed in his office, cutting down on the need for restaurant meals or grocery runs that would otherwise be part of maintaining a separate residence.

By his own estimate, the arrangement saves him roughly $1,500 a month — money that would otherwise go toward rent, utilities, and the general cost of maintaining a second home in one of the country's more expensive housing markets. Multiply that over the course of a term, and the savings add up to a substantial sum, all funneled back into personal savings rather than the D.C. rental market.

But for Chaffetz, the decision is about more than just his own bottom line. He has framed it as part of a broader statement about fiscal responsibility, one he believes should extend to the halls of Congress itself. With the national debt hovering around $10 trillion, Chaffetz argues that lawmakers should be willing to model the same kind of belt-tightening they so often demand of the federal government and, by extension, of taxpayers.

"If we're going to ask the American people to tighten their belts, to live within their means, then those of us who write the laws and appropriate the money ought to be willing to do the same," he has explained. "This is a small thing, sleeping on a cot instead of renting an apartment, but it's a reminder to myself — and hopefully to others — that we can't ask for sacrifice from the public while living comfortably at their expense."

The choice has drawn attention both for its novelty and for what it symbolizes. In a city often criticized for perks, privileges, and a disconnect between elected officials and the constituents they serve, Chaffetz's Spartan living arrangement stands out as an unusual — if pointed — gesture. Whether or not other members follow his lead, the freshman congressman has made clear that for him, the cot in the corner of his office is as much a statement as it is a bed.

# Congressman Continues Sleeping in Office, Says It Keeps Him 'Connected to Real Americans'

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — For most members of Congress, the end of a long legislative day means a commute home. For Rep. Daniel Ostrowski (R-OH), it means unfolding a cot behind his desk.

Ostrowski, 44, has slept in his Rayburn House Office Building suite since arriving in Washington six years ago — a practice he says saves money and keeps him grounded, even as ethics watchdogs and building custodians alike have raised eyebrows.

"I represent people who are working two jobs just to make rent," Ostrowski said in an interview Tuesday, gesturing to the navy blue sleeping bag tucked behind a filing cabinet. "The least I can do is not spend $2,500 a month on a D.C. apartment I'm barely in."

Ostrowski is one of roughly a dozen lawmakers known to bunk in their offices, a practice that dates back decades but has drawn renewed scrutiny in recent years. Critics say it blurs the line between public and private space in a government building, while supporters call it a refreshingly frugal alternative to Washington excess.

"It's basically a dorm room with better lighting," said one former staffer, who asked not to be named. "There's a shower schedule in the House gym. You learn to work around it."

The congressman showers each morning at the members-only gym in the Rayburn basement, keeps a rotation of suits in a closet by the door, and relies on a small refrigerator stocked with string cheese and protein bars. His office, visitors note, smells faintly of coffee and dryer sheets.

Government watchdog groups have periodically called for stricter rules around the practice, arguing it raises questions about the use of taxpayer-funded facilities for personal living arrangements. The Congressional Office of Compliance has said the practice does not technically violate any building rules, though it "discourages" it for hygiene and safety reasons.

Ostrowski shrugs off the criticism.

"I'm not asking anyone to pay for my mortgage," he said. "I go home to Dayton most weekends. This just means I'm not wasting the district's money on a fancy apartment during the week."

His office has become something of a curiosity on Capitol Hill tours, with staffers occasionally pointing out the cot to visiting constituents. Ostrowski keeps a hand-lettered sign on his door that reads: "Yes, I really sleep here."

Whether the practice is a genuine act of fiscal restraint or a savvy piece of political branding is, as with most things in Washington, a matter of perspective. But for now, Ostrowski shows no signs of trading his cot for a lease.

"Ask my back in ten years," he laughed. "But for now, it works."

Still, few have made it as central to their political identity as Whitfield.

"It's not just where I sleep," he said. "It's a daily reminder of why I'm here. Every morning I fold up that cot, I think about the debt, about the deficit, about the fact that we're spending money we don't have."

Government watchdog groups estimate the practice saves individual lawmakers somewhere between $1,500 and $2,500 a month in rent — a rounding error against a federal budget measured in trillions, and critics are quick to point that out.

## The Skeptics Push Back

Not everyone is impressed.

"It's a nice story. It makes for good local news back home," said Meredith Okafor, a public policy analyst at a Washington think tank. "But let's be honest — sleeping in an office doesn't move the needle on a $34 trillion national debt. It's theater. Effective theater, maybe, but theater."

Others raise more practical concerns. House office buildings weren't designed as residences. There have been complaints over the years about lawmakers' hygiene, about the ethics of using taxpayer-funded custodial staff to clean what amounts to a bedroom, and about whether the arrangement creates security or fire-code issues.

Whitfield brushes off the criticism. "Nobody's cleaning up after me," he said. "I do my own laundry at a laundromat two Metro stops away. I'm not asking anyone to accommodate me."

## More Than a Gimmick?

Supporters argue the optics matter precisely because so little else does in a capital where trust in institutions has eroded.

"People don't believe Washington understands sacrifice," said former congressional aide Tom Reyes. "Whether or not the cot saves real money, it tells voters something: this guy isn't here to get rich or get comfortable. That's worth something, even if it's symbolic."

Whitfield has parlayed the arrangement into a broader platform. He has co-sponsored legislation to trim congressional expense accounts, pushed for zero-based budgeting reviews across federal agencies, and repeatedly voted against omnibus spending packages — often to the frustration of his own leadership.

He's quick to reject any suggestion that he's angling for a viral moment. "I didn't do this for attention," he said. "I did it because I couldn't justify spending two grand a month on an apartment I'd barely use, paid for partly by people back home who are choosing between groceries and gas."

## The Limits of the Metaphor

Even Whitfield concedes that his living arrangement is not fiscal policy — it's a personal choice dressed up as one.

"I'm not naive," he said. "Me sleeping on a cot isn't going to balance the budget. But if a guy in Congress can't tighten his own belt, how's he going to ask the country to tighten theirs?"

Whether that logic holds up under scrutiny is, perhaps, beside the point. In an era of eroding public trust, Whitfield has found a way to make austerity legible — one folded cot at a time.
